_comment: THE CORE DATASET. Each record is one change you can make, tied to one defect, with the conditions it applies under and how confident we are. Ordered by 'order' — 1 is what to try first. 'evidence.verified' counts real submitted results and starts at zero for everything; it is never estimated, never rounded up, and never displayed as anything other than what it is. Confidence levels: 'established' = documented by manufacturers and consistent across the field; 'likely' = widely effective but with known exceptions; 'situational' = works for a specific cause only. appliesTo '*' means all.

confidenceLevels.established: Documented in manufacturer guidance and consistent across machines and materials.
confidenceLevels.likely: Widely effective, with known exceptions noted in the reasoning.
confidenceLevels.situational: Only fixes one specific underlying cause. Check that cause applies before changing anything.

fixes.amount: Per material — see the material page
fixes.title: Dry the filament before changing any setting
fixes.why: Water in the filament boils in the melt zone and forces molten plastic out of the nozzle during travel moves. No retraction value can hold back steam pressure. This is the single most common cause of sudden stringing on a material that printed fine last month, and it is the reason to check it first — every other fix on this list is wasted effort on wet filament.

fixes.amount: 5–10 °C at a time
fixes.title: Lower the nozzle temperature
fixes.why: Hotter plastic is less viscous and oozes more readily. Dropping in small steps raises viscosity enough to stop the ooze without losing layer adhesion. Go too far and you trade stringing for weak layer bonding and under-extrusion, so move in small increments and stop as soon as the strings do.

fixes.amount: 0.5 mm at a time, up to about 7 mm
fixes.title: Increase retraction distance
fixes.why: On a Bowden machine the filament has to be pulled back far enough to relieve pressure along the whole length of the tube, which is why useful values are several millimetres rather than fractions of one. Past roughly 7 mm you start grinding the filament and introducing gaps at the start of the next extrusion.

fixes.amount: 0.2 mm at a time, rarely above 2 mm
fixes.title: Increase retraction distance slightly
fixes.why: A direct-drive extruder sits millimetres from the melt zone, so tiny retractions are enough. Values borrowed from Bowden profiles are a common cause of clicking, grinding and heat creep on these machines — if you are above 2 mm and still stringing, the cause is almost certainly moisture or temperature instead.

fixes.amount: To 150–250 mm/s if the machine allows
fixes.title: Travel faster between islands
fixes.why: Any ooze that does happen gets stretched into a thinner strand and is more likely to break cleanly. This does not stop the ooze, it just gives it less time to form a bridge — which is why it is a finishing touch rather than a fix.

fixes.amount: Set to 'within infill' or 'not on outer surface'
fixes.title: Keep travel moves inside the part
fixes.why: If the nozzle never crosses open air over a visible surface, ooze lands on infill where nobody sees it. This hides stringing rather than curing it, which is entirely acceptable on a part that has to look good but not on one where the ooze is a symptom of wet filament.

fixes.amount: 5 °C at a time, within the material range
fixes.title: Raise the bed temperature
fixes.why: Warping is differential shrinkage — the bottom of the part is held flat and hot while the top cools and contracts, and the resulting stress peels the corners up. A hotter bed keeps the lower layers above their glass transition longer so they relieve stress instead of storing it.

fixes.amount: Close the chamber and stop any airflow across the printer
fixes.title: Stop the draught
fixes.why: A cold draught across one side of a part cools it faster than the other, and the part curls toward the cold side. For ABS, ASA, PC and nylon this is usually the whole explanation. Still air matters more than hot air — an unheated closed box outperforms an open printer in a heated room.

fixes.amount: To 0–20% for high-shrinkage materials
fixes.title: Turn the part cooling down
fixes.why: Cooling fans exist to freeze overhangs quickly, which is exactly the wrong thing to do to a material that shrinks as it cools. For ABS, ASA and PC the fan is often the direct cause. PLA is the opposite case and wants full cooling.

fixes.amount: 5–10 mm, or 20 mm for large flat ABS parts
fixes.title: Add a brim
fixes.why: A brim increases the bonded area at the corners, which is where peeling starts. It treats the symptom rather than the stress, but it is reliable and costs a few grams. Large flat parts in high-shrinkage materials may need a brim regardless of how good everything else is.

fixes.amount: Round or chamfer sharp bottom corners
fixes.title: Round the corners of the footprint
fixes.why: Stress concentrates at sharp corners, which is why warping almost always starts there. A 3–5 mm radius on the bottom outline spreads that stress along a curve. This is a design change rather than a setting, and on stubborn large parts it works when nothing else does.

fixes.amount: Warm water and dish soap, then dry
fixes.title: Wash the bed with soap and water
fixes.why: Skin oil from handling parts is the most common adhesion failure and isopropyl alcohol does not remove it — IPA spreads a thin film of oil rather than lifting it. Dish soap and warm water do. Do this before touching a single setting; it costs two minutes and solves the problem more often than anything else here.

fixes.amount: 0.02–0.05 mm at a time
fixes.title: Bring the nozzle slightly closer
fixes.why: A correct first layer is slightly squashed — the extrusion should be pressed into a flat-topped oval, not laid down as a round bead. If you can see gaps between first-layer lines, the nozzle is too high. Move in very small steps; too close causes elephant foot and can scrape the sheet.

fixes.amount: To 20–30 mm/s
fixes.title: Slow the first layer down
fixes.why: Slower extrusion gives the plastic time to flow into the texture of the sheet and to stay molten against a hot surface for longer. It costs a minute or two on a multi-hour print, which makes it one of the cheapest changes available.

fixes.amount: Match the sheet to the material
fixes.title: Use the right build surface for the material
fixes.why: Adhesion is a property of the pair, not of the material alone. PETG bonds to bare smooth PEI so aggressively that it can tear chunks out of the sheet, while nylon barely sticks to PEI at all and wants Garolite. Check the material page for what actually works before assuming the setting is wrong.

fixes.amount: Per material — see the material page
fixes.title: Check for moisture first
fixes.why: Wet filament produces steam pockets that interrupt the flow, giving intermittent gaps that look exactly like a flow-rate problem. If the extrusion is inconsistent rather than uniformly thin, suspect moisture before adjusting the flow multiplier.

fixes.amount: 5–10 °C at a time
fixes.title: Raise the nozzle temperature
fixes.why: Plastic that is not fully molten will not flow at the rate the slicer expects, and the shortfall grows with speed. This is the most common cause of under-extrusion that appears only on fast prints — the hotend simply cannot melt filament quickly enough to keep up.

fixes.amount: Cold pull, or replace the nozzle
fixes.title: Clear a partial clog
fixes.why: A partially blocked nozzle passes some plastic but not the commanded volume, and the symptom worsens as the print goes on. If flow was correct last week and is wrong now with nothing changed, a partial clog is more likely than any setting. Abrasive filaments wear brass nozzles into the same symptom permanently.

fixes.amount: 2–5% at a time
fixes.title: Increase the flow rate
fixes.why: Only after the causes above are excluded. Flow rate is a calibration value for a specific filament and nozzle, and raising it to paper over a mechanical fault will produce over-extrusion the moment the fault is fixed. Treat a large correction here as evidence that something else is wrong.

fixes.amount: Adjust until the gear grips without flattening the filament
fixes.title: Check the extruder grip
fixes.why: Too loose and the drive gear slips; too tight and it deforms the filament into an oval that jams in the tube. Look at the filament as it leaves the extruder — you want clean tooth marks, not a flattened ribbon or polished smooth patches.

fixes.amount: Taut enough to pluck like a bass string, not so tight it loads the bearings
fixes.title: Check belt tension
fixes.why: A loose belt lets the toothed pulley skip teeth under acceleration, and the head resumes printing from a position the controller believes is correct. The offset is permanent for the rest of the print, which is why the shift appears at one height and never corrects itself.

fixes.amount: Add Z-hop, or fix the curling that caused it
fixes.title: Stop the nozzle hitting the part
fixes.why: If a corner has curled upward, the nozzle strikes it on the next pass and knocks the axis out of step. The shift is then a downstream symptom of warping, and fixing belt tension will not help. Look at whether the layer immediately below the shift was already lifting.

fixes.amount: Reduce by 25–50%
fixes.title: Reduce acceleration
fixes.why: Skipped steps happen when the motor is asked for more torque than it can deliver, and demand rises with acceleration. Bed-slingers are worse in Y because the whole heated bed and the part must reverse direction. Lowering acceleration costs print time and is the reliable fix when the machine is simply being asked for too much.

fixes.amount: Small increments, watching motor temperature
fixes.title: Raise stepper current
fixes.why: Under-powered drivers skip under load. Raising current increases torque but also heat, and a stepper hot enough to be uncomfortable to touch will skip for thermal reasons instead. Change this last and in small steps.

fixes.amount: 0.02 mm at a time
fixes.title: Raise the nozzle slightly
fixes.why: Elephant foot is the first layer being squashed wider than the layers above it. If the first layer is over-compressed the excess has nowhere to go but sideways. Move in very small steps — go too far and you trade a bulged base for a part that will not stick at all.

fixes.amount: 5 °C at a time
fixes.title: Lower the bed temperature
fixes.why: A bed hot enough to keep the lowest layers above their softening point lets the weight of the part above spread them. This is common with PLA on a bed run at 65 °C when 55 °C would do — the material never fully sets near the plate.

fixes.title: Use the slicer's compensation setting
fixes.why: Most slicers can shrink the first layer outline by a fixed amount to cancel the bulge. It corrects the dimension without disturbing a first layer that is otherwise adhering well, which makes it the right choice when adhesion is marginal and you dare not raise the nozzle.

fixes.amount: Halve it, then tune upward
fixes.title: Reduce acceleration
fixes.why: Ringing is mechanical resonance — the head changes direction, the frame rings like a struck bell, and the nozzle traces that oscillation into the surface just past each corner. Lower acceleration excites the frame less. It is the most direct fix and it costs print time.

fixes.amount: Run the machine's calibration routine
fixes.title: Calibrate input shaping
fixes.why: Input shaping measures the frame's resonant frequency and shapes the motion commands to cancel it, which removes ringing without giving up speed. Where the firmware supports it this is strictly better than lowering acceleration. Where it does not, it is not an option.

fixes.amount: Tighten frame bolts, brace the gantry, move off a flexing surface
fixes.title: Stiffen the machine
fixes.why: A printer on a flexing desk or IKEA shelf will ring no matter what the settings say, because the resonating mass includes the furniture. Loose frame bolts and an unbraced gantry do the same. Check this before spending an evening tuning numbers that cannot win.

fixes.amount: 5–10 °C at a time
fixes.title: Raise the nozzle temperature
fixes.why: Layers bond by the new extrusion partially re-melting the one beneath it. Too cold and they sit against each other without fusing, giving a part that splits cleanly along a layer line under load. This is the first thing to change and usually the only one needed.

fixes.amount: To 0–30% depending on material
fixes.title: Turn the cooling down
fixes.why: Cooling air freezes the previous layer before the next one arrives, which is precisely what prevents fusion. High-temperature materials want almost no part cooling for this reason. PLA is the exception and tolerates full cooling because it bonds at low temperature.

fixes.amount: Close the chamber, block any airflow
fixes.title: Eliminate draughts
fixes.why: A cold draught does the same thing as a cooling fan, only unpredictably and on one side of the part. Splitting that appears on the side facing a window or a door is this, not a settings problem.

fixes.amount: To 75% of nozzle diameter or less
fixes.title: Reduce the layer height
fixes.why: Thinner layers put more surface area in contact and squash harder against the layer below, both of which improve bonding. A layer height close to the nozzle diameter gives a nearly round bead with little contact area, which is weak by construction.

fixes.amount: To 100% where the material allows
fixes.title: Increase part cooling
fixes.why: An overhang is extruded partly into open air and must solidify before gravity pulls it down. More cooling means less time hanging. This conflicts directly with layer adhesion on high-temperature materials, which is why good overhangs in ABS are genuinely hard rather than a settings oversight.

fixes.amount: To 50% of normal perimeter speed
fixes.title: Slow down over overhangs
fixes.why: Slower extrusion over open air gives the fan longer to set each millimetre before the next arrives. Most slicers have a dedicated overhang speed so the rest of the print keeps its pace.

fixes.amount: Rotate so overhangs stay under 45°
fixes.title: Reorient the part
fixes.why: Below roughly 45° each layer is still supported by more than half of the one beneath it and no bridging is required. Rotating the model is free, needs no support material, and produces a better surface than any amount of tuning.
